Project review
Twin in the Loop
A digital twin that vets every repair an AI proposes, before the network feels it.
Start here · no background needed

A small network breaks. An AI proposes a fix. Something has to check the fix first.

Every number, chart, prompt and model reply on this page was produced by running the code in this repository. Nothing is illustrative or mocked up. Where a result is awkward for the project, it is shown anyway and labelled.

Imagine a handful of small computers at the edge of a network — the kind that sit in a factory, a hospital, or a phone mast — running six services that have to answer requests quickly. Things go wrong on their own: a processor gets pinned, a machine dies, a cable degrades, a program leaks memory, traffic spikes.

An agent watches the symptoms and proposes a repair. It is never told what actually broke; it only sees latency, utilisation and dropped requests, exactly like a real on-call engineer looking at a dashboard.

Here is the catch this whole project exists for: repairs can make things worse. Moving a service to another machine takes it offline while it moves. Restarting it throws away the queue. An agent that confidently does the wrong thing is more dangerous than one that does nothing.

So before a repair touches the real network, it is tried out on a digital twin — a copy of the network that is deliberately imperfect, because real twins always are. If the twin predicts the repair will hurt, the repair is rejected and the agent is told why, and gets another try.

The research question How good does the twin have to be before this checking step is worth its cost? A perfect twin obviously helps — but a perfect twin is not a twin, it is the thing itself. The interesting answer is the point where a blurry twin stops paying for itself.
You can run this, not just read it Start the local server and the section executes a complete episode on your machine and streams every part of it to the page as it happens — ticks, faults, prompts, model replies, twin forecasts and the ground truth that grades them. Everything else here is a recording of exactly that.

The loop, end to end

Click any stage to jump to the level that builds it.

What the twelve levels are

The project was built in twelve strictly ordered levels. Each level has a hard exit criterion: if its test does not pass, the level is not finished and the next one does not start. That rule is the reason the results at the end can be trusted — nothing downstream is built on an unverified foundation.

Verified while building this page uv run pytest -q → 107 passed, across thirteen test modules — one per level, plus one for the live streaming layer. Every “exit criterion met” badge on this page is that suite, not a claim.

The headline numbers

From a five-seed comparison run for this review, 120 ticks per episode, identical fault schedules across every arm. Full detail in and .

Words this page uses

How to read this page honestly Most results here come from five seeds, not the thirty the paper plan calls for. That is enough to show the mechanism clearly and not enough for error bars. Wherever a number is thin, small, or points the wrong way, it says so on the spot.
Level 01 · Scaffold

Same seed, same universe, every single time

Builds the repository skeleton, the validated configuration system, and the seed manager that makes every experiment exactly repeatable.

Exit criterion met Two managers from one master seed produce identical streams tests/test_seeding.py · 5 tests passing

Nothing else in this project works if this does not. The whole method rests on being able to ask "what would have happened if we had done nothing instead?" — and you can only ask that if you can rewind the universe and replay it exactly.

Randomness in the simulator never comes from a global random number generator. Every random thing — when requests arrive, how long each takes, which packets are lost — draws from its own named stream, derived from one master seed by hashing the stream's name. So the arrival stream for svc0 is independent of the service-time stream for svc3, and drawing from one never disturbs the other.

Try it

Two managers built from the same master seed, and one built from a different master. First five numbers from three different named streams.

Why order-independence matters

A naive design would hand out one generator and let callers draw from it in turn. Then adding a single extra draw anywhere — a new metric, a debug print — shifts every subsequent random number and silently changes the whole experiment. Here, asking for a stream by name always gives you the same generator at the same starting position, no matter what else has been drawn.

Forking the seed, not sharing it

When the simulator forks a copy of itself — which Level 3 makes possible and the twin depends on — the child needs its own randomness, derived from the parent so it is reproducible, but independent so the two do not march in lockstep forever. child(label) does that: the same label always derives the same child, different labels never collide.

Level 02 · Core simulator

A network you can watch, one tick at a time

Builds the nodes, links, services and workload, and the tick loop with its fixed six-stage update order.

Exit criterion met tests/test_sim.py · 3 tests passing

The simulator is a custom discrete-tick engine, written from scratch rather than borrowed from an off-the-shelf network simulator. That was a deliberate trade: existing simulators make deep-copy forking and controlled degradation awkward, and forking is the single capability this entire project is built on.

The network being simulated

One gateway, four edge servers, twelve devices, six services. Hover any part of it. Small enough to run hundreds of episodes; large enough that deciding where to put a service is a real decision.

Topology · small (v1)

What happens in one tick

The order is fixed and must never vary — if it did, the same seed would stop producing the same episode. One tick is one second of simulated time.

A healthy network, 120 ticks, no faults

This is the baseline behaviour with nothing wrong. Latency and utilisation settle and stay settled. Drag the slider to scrub through time; the numbers under the chart are the live state at that tick.

Proof of determinism

The same seed, run twice, from scratch. Mean p95 response time for the first twenty ticks, to six decimal places.

Level 03 · Fork and snapshot

Copying a running network without disturbing it

Builds snapshot, restore and fork — the operation that makes both the digital twin and the ground truth possible.

Exit criterion met tests/test_fork.py · 8 tests passing

This is the load-bearing level. Two different things in this project need to run a copy of the network forward in time: the twin, which predicts what a repair would do, and the counterfactual, which afterwards establishes what the repair really would have done. Both are forks.

A fork must share nothing at all with its parent. Not a list, not a dictionary, not a queue of pending requests, and above all not the state of a random number generator — because two simulators sharing one generator would drift apart the moment either of them drew a number.

Fork, then run both forward untouched

Fork at tick 50, then step the parent and both children thirty ticks with no intervention. If the copy is genuine, all three traces are identical, number for number.

Break the child, check the parent

Now fork at tick 50 again and take a node down in the child only. The child's trace diverges immediately. The parent's state is then compared field by field against a snapshot taken before the fork existed.

Snapshot and restore

Snapshot at tick 20, run 25 ticks, restore, run the same 25 ticks again. Identical sequences means the snapshot captured everything, generator states included.

Independent randomness, proven

A fork inherits the parent's generator position — that is what makes the untouched traces match. But its SeedManager is a derived child, so any new stream it creates is genuinely its own. Both facts are visible here.

Level 04 · Fault injection

Six ways for things to go wrong, on a schedule you can replay

Builds the fault catalogue, seeded fault schedules, and the injector that applies and reverts events at exact ticks.

Exit criterion met tests/test_faults.py · 10 tests passing

Faults are generated from the seed, not chosen by hand. That matters more than it sounds: it means arm A0 and arm A3 face exactly the same disasters at exactly the same ticks, so any difference in outcome is caused by the agent, not by luck. It also means nobody can be accused of picking faults the AI happens to be good at.

Same seed, same disasters

A schedule is three faults per episode by default, each with a type, a target, a start tick, a duration and a magnitude. Change the seed and you get a different world; use the same seed twice and you get the same world.

What each fault actually looks like from the outside

This is the part that makes the agent's job hard. Pick a fault below to inject it at tick 30 for forty ticks and watch the symptoms. Only two of the six make the network look slow. The others make it look quiet, or look completely normal.

The six signatures side by side

Average values before the fault and while it is active. The agent sees these columns and nothing else — never the fault's name.

A finding worth stating plainly A memory leak barely moves latency in this simulator, because memory is not on the path that determines service speed. It only bites indirectly, by filling a node so that a later migration or scale-up gets refused. So the rule agent's leak detector watches memory growth directly rather than waiting for a latency signal that never comes.
Level 05 · Telemetry and SLO

Turning a wall of numbers into something worth reading

Builds the collector that structures an observation, the SLO evaluator that decides what counts as broken, and the summarizer that renders it inside a token budget.

Exit criterion met tests/test_telemetry.py · 5 tests passing

Collection and summarising are deliberately separate stages. The rule agent eats the structured form directly; the language model gets the rendered text. That split means the text representation can be redesigned without touching a line of simulator code.

What counts as broken

Raw telemetry on the left, what the model is handed on the right

Pick a moment. The left column is the complete TickMetrics and SLO evaluation the collector produced. The right column is the exact text the summarizer renders from it — the only thing the language model ever sees about the state of the network.

Notice what is missing The rendered text names symptoms and never names causes. There is no line saying "edge0 is saturated". The agent has to work that out. That is the whole point — a diagnosis benchmark, not a fill-in-the-blank exercise.

The token budget

A raw dump of every metric from twenty-three nodes, seventeen links and six services would cost a fortune per decision and would reason worse, not better. The summarizer prioritises: services in violation first, then services at risk, then hot nodes, then elevated links; healthy services collapse to one aggregate line if the budget is tight.

Level 06 · Actions

A closed set of repairs, checked three times before anything happens

Builds the action schema, the three-layer validator, and the executor that models real downtime and transfer cost.

Exit criterion met Every action type applies with the right effect Invalid actions rejected before execution tests/test_actions.py · 10 tests passing

The language model never writes commands into the simulator. It picks one of six actions from a fixed schema and fills in the parameters. Anything outside that schema is rejected at the door and logged as a malformed-action event — itself a number worth reporting, because it measures how often the model fails to follow instructions.

Three layers of checking

The six actions, and what each one costs

Pick an action to apply it to a live simulator at tick 40 and watch the twenty-five ticks that follow. Note that the two most powerful repairs are also the two that take the service offline while they work.

Layer 1 — does it even parse?

Real payloads run through the Pydantic schema. Note that unknown fields are refused too, not silently dropped: extra="forbid" means a model that invents a parameter is caught rather than obeyed halfway.

Layer 2 — does it make sense here and now?

Parsing is not enough. migrate_service to a machine with no memory left is perfectly well-formed and completely wrong. Every one of these was run against real simulator state.

Level 07 · Baseline agents

The conventional operator, tuned to be beatable only fairly

Builds the threshold-driven rule agent and the null agent, both behind one shared interface.

Exit criterion met Rule agent recovers a CPU saturation fault end to end All tuning lives in config, not in code tests/test_agents.py · 7 tests passing

A reviewer will assume the baseline was weakened on purpose. So the rule agent's every threshold is written down, justified, and kept in the config file where anyone can change it and re-run. It is a genuine attempt at a good conventional operator, not a strawman.

The rule ladder

Checked strictly in this order. The first rule that fires wins; if none fire, the agent holds.

Every threshold, and why it has that value

The four safeguards that stop it thrashing

Watch it decide

A full 120-tick episode, seed 15. Each row is one decision point. The reason text is the agent's own explanation, generated at the moment it decided.

Kept on purpose The rule agent sometimes acts when riding out a blip would have been better, and a crashed node reads as low utilisation, so its migrate rule never fires for the fault that most needs it. These weaknesses are documented rather than patched. Removing them would hide the exact phenomenon the project studies: acting without checking consequences is risky.
Level 08 · LLM layer and agent

Exactly what goes to the model, and exactly what comes back

Builds the provider abstraction, response caching, budget guard, structured-output enforcement, and the ReAct agent with read-only telemetry tools.

Exit criterion met Schema-valid actions from real telemetry Every call traced: latency, tokens, cache tests/test_llm_agent.py · 11 tests passing

This is the level to look at closely, because it is where an AI project is usually hand-waved. Nothing below is paraphrased. Every message array and every reply is the real payload, replayed from the cached transcript of the recorded run.

The instruction file, verbatim

Prompts are versioned files on disk, never strings buried in code, and the version goes into every log record. This is agent/prompts/llm_agent_v1.txt in full — the entire system message, nothing removed.

System prompt · v1

  


  
The ReAct loop

  
The model may investigate before deciding. Each turn it returns one JSON object: either a tool call, which the agent answers with real telemetry, or a final action. It gets a limited number of turns.

  


  
The conversation inspector

  
Pick a decision, then step through the turns. Sent shows the complete message array that went to the provider — the system prompt, the observation, and every tool result so far. Received shows the model's raw reply text before any parsing.

  


  
What the tools return

  
Four read-only tools. They cannot change anything — they only expose what a real operator could query. Each returns a JSON blob that is pasted straight into the conversation as a user message.

  


  
Cost and caching

  
Every call is logged with its latency and token counts. Identical prompts hit a content-addressed cache, which is what makes the whole analysis reproducible offline — and is why this page can show real model output without calling anything.

Level 09 · Twin and fidelity

    
The check itself, and the five ways it is allowed to be wrong

    
Builds the twin validator — fork, degrade, apply, roll forward, compare against doing nothing — and the five fidelity axes with the scalar that drives them.

    

      Exit criterion met
      At fidelity 1.0 the twin's prediction matches reality exactly
      Degraded fidelity diverges as designed
      tests/test_twin.py · 11 tests passing
    

  


  
This is the contribution. Everything before it exists so that this step can be measured properly.


  
What the validator does, in five steps

  


  

    The approval rule, deliberately simple
    Approve if the predicted SLO violations from acting are no worse than from doing nothing, within a tolerance. A clever approval rule would become an unexplainable confound — when the result changed, nobody could say whether the twin or the rule caused it.
  


  
The five ways a twin is imperfect

  
A twin that matches reality exactly is not a twin, it is the network. Real twins are built from noisy monitoring, sync late, drift out of calibration, simplify their models for speed, and guess at future demand. Each of those is a knob here.

  


  
Turn the dial

  
One scalar drives all five axes. Move it and watch the twin's judgement change on five real candidate actions, all evaluated at the same moment of the same episode — a CPU-saturated edge server at tick 35, with the fault hidden from everyone.

  


  
A prediction next to the truth

  
For the selected candidate: what the twin forecast, and what a fork of the real simulator says actually would have happened.

  


  
Watch an episode happen

  
The same network from Level 2, now with faults firing and an agent working. Press play, or drag the slider. Edge servers redden as their CPU fills; a service turns red when it breaks its SLO; a link turns dashed red when it fails. The banner tells you what is really wrong — something the agent is never told.

  


  
The twin catching something, in a real episode

  
Seed 15, LLM agent, twin at fidelity 1.0. Step through the decisions. Two of them are rejections that the ground truth later confirms were correct; one is a miss.

  


  

    Fidelity 1.0 is not omniscience
    Even a perfect fork rolls forward fault-blind: it cannot see faults that have not happened yet, and it does not know when an active fault will end. So a perfect twin still misses harm caused by the future rather than by the action. That is realistic — no twin can forecast an unannounced hardware failure — and it puts a ceiling on how well this method can ever do.
  







  

    
Level 10 · LangGraph orchestration

    
The whole loop as a state machine, with the rejection edge wired in

    
Builds the state graph — observe, propose, validate, execute, finalise — with the conditional retry edge, a retry cap, a no-op fallback, and SQLite checkpointing.

    

      Exit criterion met
      Full episode runs with faults, rejections and recoveries
      Graph diagram exports to docs/graph.mmd
      tests/test_graph.py · 10 tests passing
    

  


  
Up to here the pieces existed separately. This level wires them into one graph, so the retry behaviour is a property of the structure rather than of a loop buried in a function. Turning the twin off is a structural change — one edge is rerouted from validate straight to execute — which is exactly what makes arm A2 and arm A3 a fair comparison.


  
The graph

  


  
What each node does

  


  
Walk a real decision through it

  
Captured by streaming the graph's state after every node. Decision points from a live episode — the first one contains a rejection, so you can watch the state travel back to propose with the twin's reason attached.

  


  
Why a retry cap exists

  
Without one, an agent that keeps proposing rejected actions loops forever. With one, the loop gives up after  retries and applies no_op, and the record is flagged exhausted — which is itself a measurable outcome rather than a hidden failure.

  







  

    
Level 11 · Experiment runner

    
Six arms, identical disasters, and the ground truth for every idea

    
Builds the arm definitions, the seed sweep, the offline counterfactual fork path, structured JSONL logging, and resumable checkpointing.

    

      Exit criterion met
      All arms run across seeds
      Every decision record carries a counterfactual outcome
      tests/test_experiment.py · 11 tests passing
    

  


  
The arms, and what each one is for

  


  

    Arm A4 is the one reviewers ask for
    Rule agent plus twin. Without it, anyone can claim the result is really about validation-in-general and has nothing to do with AI. With it, the AI's contribution and the twin's contribution can be told apart.
  


  
How we know an action was harmful

  
Not by guessing, and not by asking the twin. Before the agent acts, the real simulator is forked. Every proposal it makes — including the ones the twin rejected, which never touched the network — is replayed on that fork with the real fault schedule intact, and compared against replaying nothing. The difference in SLO violation-ticks is the ground-truth label.

  


  
Results across five seeds

  
Every arm faces identical fault schedules. 120 ticks, a decision every 10 ticks, 20-tick prediction horizon. Lower violation-ticks is better.

Level 12 · Analysis

    
Was the twin right, and did being right pay for itself?

    
Builds metric computation, the twin confusion matrix, the fidelity sweep and the figures — all regenerated from logs, without re-querying any model.

How this page was produced

  
Every figure comes from scripts that import the project's own modules and run them. Simulator results are deterministic, so re-running reproduces them exactly. The language-model exchanges are replayed from the content-addressed response cache committed in the repository, so no call was made to any provider while building this page.
